summary:
Paul Copplestone introduces Supabase as a backend-as-a-service platform whose tagline is "build in a weekend, scale to millions." The platform provides full Postgres databases along with authentication, edge functions (Deno-powered), file storage, realtime systems, and a vector offering powered by pgvector. Supabase is open source (MIT, Apache 2, or Postgres licensed) and supports existing communities.

The pgvector story began when Greg emailed asking Supabase to accept a Postgres extension for vector operations. Within a day it was merged, and within two weeks they launched "clippy," an AI-powered doc search interface. Greg now works at Supabase. pgvector became a major growth tailwind—Supabase now launches around 12,000 databases per week, with 10-15% using pgvector. One app scaled to a million users in 10 days after being built in 3 days.

A performance challenge arose from a tweet claiming pgvector was 20x slower than Qdrant and 18% worse at finding relevant docs. Andrew Kane, the original pgvector contributor, along with Supabase, Qdrant, and AWS teams, built an HNSW index in about one month. Results showed both queries per second and accuracy improved, reaching 0.99 accuracy. An apples-to-apples comparison with Pinecone showed Postgres offering better queries per second at similar compute cost ($410 vs $480 for six Pinecone replicas).

Paul demonstrates a content moderation use case using Postgres partitions. The example segments "good cats" from "bad cats" by comparing uploaded image embeddings against a canonical "Space Cat" using a similarity threshold of 0.8. A trigger function runs on every insert, comparing embeddings and routing them to appropriate partitions. This approach, achievable in roughly 14 lines of SQL, leverages Postgres's built-in features: good cat partitions get indexed for fast queries, while bad cat partitions can be dropped and recreated for cleanup.

Paul's broader argument is that Postgres's extensibility, 30 years of engineering, row-level security for RAG applications, and the advantage of single round trips (storing embeddings alongside other data) make it a powerful vector database choice. He notes pgvector is currently an extension but may eventually be merged into Postgres core. He acknowledges specialized vector databases still have a place for use cases Postgres won't handle, such as putting models closer to the database. Looking ahead, Supabase is focused on enterprise use cases, particularly storing billions of vectors. They are developing sharding with Citus, a Postgres extension, which allows splitting data across nodes with transactions scaling linearly as nodes are added. Supabase is collaborating with the Citus team at Microsoft and seeking design partners already storing billions of embeddings.

sections.title: Introduction to Supabase and pgvector
sections.summary: Paul introduces Supabase as an open-source backend-as-a-service built on Postgres, offering authentication, edge functions, file storage, realtime, and vector storage powered by pgvector. He explains how Greg emailed to propose merging the pgvector extension, which was accepted within a day, leading to the launch of 'clippy' (AI doc search) two weeks later.

sections.title: Growth and Adoption of pgvector
sections.summary: A chart shows pgvector accelerating Supabase's database growth. They now launch ~12,000 databases/week with 10-15% using pgvector. One app scaled to a million users in 10 days. The conference app is powered by Supabase. Greg now works at Supabase.

sections.title: Performance Controversy and HNSW Response
sections.summary: A tweet claimed pgvector was 20x slower than Qdrant and 18% worse at relevance. Andrew Kane (pgvector creator) and teams from Supabase, Qdrant, and AWS built an HNSW index in about a month, improving both queries per second and accuracy to 0.99. An apples-to-apples comparison showed Postgres ($410) outperforming Pinecone's 6 replicas ($480).

sections.title: Content Moderation Demonstration with Postgres Partitions
sections.summary: Paul demonstrates using Postgres partitions for content moderation. A canonical 'Space Cat' embedding is used to compare uploaded cat images via an is_cat function with a 0.8 similarity threshold. A trigger runs on insert, routing embeddings to good or bad cat partitions. Good cats are indexed; bad cats can be dropped for cleanup. The solution requires approximately 14 lines of SQL.

sections.title: Why Postgres for Vector Workloads
sections.summary: Paul argues Postgres's 30 years of engineering, extensibility, and built-in primitives make it ideal for AI applications. He highlights row-level security for RAG applications and the advantage of single round trips by co-locating embeddings with other data. He notes pgvector is currently an extension but may eventually merge into Postgres core. He acknowledges specialized vector databases still have a place for use cases like putting models closer to the database, but for storing, indexing, and fetching embeddings, Postgres is moving in that direction.

sections.title: Future Directions: Enterprise Scale and Sharding
sections.summary: Paul outlines Supabase's focus on enterprise use cases, particularly storing billions of vectors. They are developing sharding with Citus, a Postgres extension, to split data across nodes, with transactions scaling linearly as nodes are added. Supabase is collaborating with the Citus team at Microsoft and seeking design partners already storing billions of embeddings. He invites developers to get started at database.new and mentions swag available at the booth.
